script.opening: "I feel like I’m going mad. For a week or two before my period I turn into a different person — furious over nothing, then this black despair, crying, snapping at my partner and kids. I’ve frightened myself with how low I get. Then my period comes and within a day or two it just… lifts, and I’m fine. My last doctor said it’s just bad PMS. It’s wrecking my life."

facts.text: Builds up about 10 days, sometimes 2 weeks, before each period. Furious over small things, then "black despair", crying, anxious, can’t concentrate, wants to hide under the duvet. Within a day or two of the period starting, "like a light switches back on". Fine the rest of the month. Has been like this for about 3 years, worse since her second child.
Bloating, sore breasts, craving sweet food, poor sleep in that week. Periods regular, 28 days, not especially heavy. No bleeding between periods or after sex.

facts.topic: Mood the rest of the month (if asked)
facts.text: Good. Enjoys things, sleeps well, no anxiety. Never had a long spell of low mood. Never had a time of being "high", needing no sleep or spending wildly.

"Sometimes I’ve thought everyone would be better off without me." Only in the week before her period; no plan, never acted on it, "it goes when my period comes. I’d never leave the kids." No self-harm.

Partner had a vasectomy; not using hormones. Not breastfeeding. No medicines, no allergies. No migraine with aura. Non-smoker, BMI 24. Drinks "too much wine that week, to calm down" — about a bottle over the week.

Lives with partner, Rhys, and two children (7 and 4). Works part-time as a dental nurse; took two days off last month. Mother had "bad nerves" after having children. Rhys is supportive but they row every month.
Has never kept a symptom diary. Has a period-tracker app on her phone.

Articulate, upset, slightly defensive at first because last time you were dismissed. If the doctor takes you seriously, become tearful with relief. Reveal the dark thoughts only if asked directly and kindly. Ask: "Do I have to wait two months for help, though?" if a diary is suggested. Prefer not to take hormones.

ice.ideas: "Either I’m going mad, or I’m just a horrible person that week."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — guilt about how she treats the children, and fear of how low she gets: "I scare myself."
ice.expectations: "For someone to take it seriously, and something that actually helps."

cues: "My last doctor said it’s just bad PMS" — she has felt dismissed before.
"I’ve frightened myself with how low I get" — the door to asking about suicidal thoughts.
"Within a day or two it just lifts" — the cyclical pattern that points to the diagnosis.

checkpoints.text: Recognises PREMENSTRUAL DYSPHORIC DISORDER — severe affective (± physical) symptoms in the LUTEAL phase that are functionally impairing and RESOLVE after menstruation with a symptom-free follicular interval
Distinguishes PMDD from ordinary (milder) PMS and from an underlying MOOD DISORDER with premenstrual exacerbation (symptoms persisting through the cycle) — the symptom-free window being the key
Confirms the pattern with a PROSPECTIVE symptom DIARY over at least 2 cycles rather than relying on retrospective recall
Assesses SEVERITY/impact and explicitly screens RISK (suicidal thoughts/self-harm, especially luteal), recognising PMDD’s genuine risk

Offers EVIDENCE-BASED treatment per RCOG GTG 48 (lifestyle; SSRI — continuous or luteal-phase, unlicensed for PMS, after a bipolar screen; new-generation combined pill after a UKMEC check; CBT) and refers to gynaecology/specialist for severe/refractory cases, with shared decision-making
VALIDATES strongly — that this is a recognised, treatable condition and NOT "just PMS"/"just hormones"/a character flaw — responding to her feeling dismissed and frightened
Explores impact on relationships/work and her preferences, explains the diagnosis and plan, and checks understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: crisis/risk safety-netting (worsening mood/suicidality, especially premenstrually), review within 1 week of starting an SSRI given her suicidal thoughts (NICE NG222), the diary and review to confirm and tailor treatment, and ongoing support — recognition + validation + evidence-based treatment, not dismissal

worked.txt: "You are not going mad, and this is not ‘just PMS’. What you’re describing — severe mood changes that build before your period and then lift once it starts — is a recognised, treatable condition called premenstrual dysphoric disorder, PMDD. I’m really sorry you were brushed off; this is real."

"The key thing that makes me confident is that you feel genuinely WELL for part of the month, then it returns predictably before your period. To be sure, I’d like you to keep a daily symptom diary over a couple of cycles — it confirms the pattern and rules out a depression that’s there all the time."

"Because you said the lows frighten you — can I ask directly: in that premenstrual week, have you had thoughts of harming yourself or that life isn’t worth living? … Thank you for telling me. That matters and we’ll keep you safe."

"The good news is there are effective treatments. An antidepressant called an SSRI works well for PMDD — and uniquely here, it can be taken either every day or just in the two weeks before your period. It isn’t officially licensed for this, which I’ll explain, but it’s the recommended treatment. Before starting, have you ever had spells of feeling unusually high or wired? A newer type of combined pill, taken continuously, can also help by smoothing the hormone swings, if it’s safe for you — I’ll ask about migraine and arrange a blood pressure check first — and talking therapy (CBT) helps too. We can choose what fits you."
"What appeals more — trying the SSRI, the hormonal route, or both alongside lifestyle changes like exercise and easing off caffeine/alcohol? Do you also need contraception, as that might steer us?"

"Keep the diary, and if you start the SSRI I’d like to speak again within a week, then review in a couple of cycles to confirm and see how treatment’s working. If your mood drops badly or you ever feel unsafe — especially before your period — contact us straight away. You’ve been carrying this alone for too long."

f.learning: PREMENSTRUAL DYSPHORIC DISORDER (PMDD) is the severe, functionally impairing end of premenstrual disorders: prominent affective symptoms (irritability/RAGE, low mood/DESPAIR, anxiety, mood swings, feeling out of control) ± physical symptoms occurring in the LUTEAL phase (the 1–2 weeks before menstruation), damaging relationships/work, and RESOLVING shortly after the period starts with a SYMPTOM-FREE follicular interval — the cyclical timing with a symptom-free window being the diagnostic key. Distinguish it from ordinary (milder, non-disabling) PMS and from an underlying MOOD DISORDER with premenstrual exacerbation, where symptoms PERSIST through the cycle (worse premenstrually) rather than fully resolving. Confirm with a PROSPECTIVE symptom DIARY over at least two cycles, since retrospective recall is unreliable and the diary both confirms PMDD and excludes a persistent mood disorder. Assess severity and functional impact, and explicitly screen RISK — PMDD causes genuine distress and carries a real suicide/self-harm risk in the luteal phase — while validating strongly that this is a recognised medical condition, NOT "just PMS"/"just hormones" or a character failing (the validation is itself therapeutic after dismissal). Offer evidence-based treatment per RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 48 (2016): lifestyle measures; an SSRI (effective in PMDD, given continuously OR only in the luteal phase; unlicensed for PMS in the UK, dose per BNF; screen for bipolar features first and review within 1 week if at increased suicide risk, NICE NG222); combined hormonal contraception/ovulation suppression (a new-generation combined pill, drospirenone-containing usually more effective, cyclical or continuous, after a UKMEC check); CBT; risk explored without risk labels and with a safety plan (NICE NG225); and referral to gynaecology/specialist for severe/refractory cases (GnRH analogues ± add-back, rarely surgery), tailored to her preferences and contraceptive needs. The hidden agenda is feeling she is "going mad" and previously dismissed; recognise, confirm, assess risk, validate, and treat with shared decision-making.

knowledge.guideline: [1] RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 48 Management of premenstrual syndrome (December 2016; BJOG 2017) · [2] NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (2022) · [3] NICE NG222 Depression in adults: treatment and management (2022, updated December 2025) · [4] UKMEC 2025 (FSRH/CoSRH) · [5] BNF: selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors · [6] DSM-5-TR (APA 2022) (international)
knowledge.summary: Severe rage, despair and tearfulness in the week or two before each period, which lift within days of bleeding, with a symptom-free week and damage to relationships, is premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), the severe end of premenstrual syndrome. The GP should believe her, confirm the cyclical pattern prospectively, rule out a persistent mood disorder, ask directly about suicidal thoughts, and offer RCOG first-line options including an SSRI (continuous or luteal phase) or a new-generation combined pill.

points.t: The main UK guideline on premenstrual syndrome is RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 48 [1]. Symptoms occur in the luteal phase, resolve by the end of menstruation, and are absent for at least a week in the follicular phase. PMDD is the severe, predominantly psychological form; the formal criteria are in DSM-5-TR [6] (international).

RCOG [1]: diagnose using prospective daily symptom ratings over two consecutive cycles, for example the Daily Record of Severity of Problems (DRSP). Retrospective recall is unreliable. A symptom-free week separates PMDD from depression or anxiety that worsens before periods.

Ask directly about suicidal thoughts and self-harm, especially in the luteal phase. NICE NG225 [2]: do not use risk tools or label risk as low, medium or high; agree a safety plan. Ask about bipolar symptoms before an SSRI.

RCOG [1] first-line options: exercise, CBT, vitamin B6, a new-generation combined oral contraceptive (drospirenone-containing pills usually more effective), taken cyclically or continuously, and low-dose SSRIs, given continuously or in the luteal phase only (days 15 to 28). SSRIs are unlicensed for PMS in the UK (dose per BNF [5]). Check UKMEC [4] before a combined pill: migraine with aura is UKMEC 4.
NICE NG222 [3]: review within 1 week of starting an antidepressant if at increased suicide risk. Withdraw gradually after continuous use; luteal-phase dosing avoids withdrawal effects.

RCOG [1]: second-line includes transdermal estradiol, off-label and usually with specialist advice (100 micrograms twice weekly is as effective as 200 micrograms) with cyclical progestogen or an LNG-IUS for endometrial protection. Specialist care for GnRH analogues (with add-back HRT if used beyond 6 months) and, rarely, surgery. Review after two to three cycles of each treatment.

dg.d: Open start; acknowledged the previous dismissal.
Relationships, parenting, guilt and work explored.
Prospective daily symptom diary over two cycles (RCOG GTG 48); no routine blood tests needed.
PMDD versus ordinary PMS, persistent depression or anxiety with premenstrual worsening, and bipolar disorder.
Suicidal thoughts, plans and self-harm explored; bipolar features screened before an SSRI.
Named PMDD as the severe form of premenstrual syndrome.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: SSRI (luteal or continuous) or new-generation combined pill offered with CBT and exercise (RCOG GTG 48); her choice respected.
Guilt and impact on the family addressed; partner involved in the safety plan with her agreement.
Review in 1 week given suicidal thoughts (NICE NG222), then after two cycles; crisis routes given; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I’ve frightened myself with how low I get” and asked directly about suicidal thoughts.
Idea (going mad or a bad person), concern (the lows and the family), expectation (to be taken seriously and helped).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — guilt about how she treats the children, and fear of how low she gets: "I scare myself." — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Miss Devlin, I’m Dr Evans. What would you like to talk about today?

I feel like I’m going mad. For a week or two before my period I turn into a different person: furious over nothing, then this black despair, crying, snapping at my partner and kids. I’ve frightened myself with how low I get. Then my period comes and within a day or two it just lifts, and I’m fine. My last doctor said it’s just bad PMS. It’s wrecking my life.
I’m sorry it’s been so hard, and that you felt brushed off before. I’d like to understand exactly what happens, so we can do something about it.
model.why: Validates and responds to feeling dismissed

model.text: When your period finishes, how are you in the week or so after? Completely yourself, or still low?
model.why: Tests for a symptom-free follicular phase

model.text: Completely fine. Like a light switches back on. That’s why it’s so confusing.
And when does it start again, compared with your period?
About ten days before, sometimes two weeks. It builds up.
Are your periods regular? Any physical symptoms at that time, like bloating or sore breasts?
Regular. Yes, I get bloated and my breasts are sore, but the moods are the real problem.
Have you ever had long spells of low mood, or times when you felt unusually high or needed little sleep, that weren’t tied to your cycle?
model.why: Screens persistent depression and bipolar features

model.text: No, only before my period.
You said you’ve frightened yourself with how low you get. Can I ask directly: in those days, have you had thoughts of harming yourself, or that life isn’t worth living?
model.why: Picks up the cue and asks about suicide directly

model.text: (quietly) Sometimes I’ve thought everyone would be better off without me. I’ve never done anything, and it goes when my period comes.
Thank you for telling me. That matters and I’m glad you said it. Have you ever made plans, or harmed yourself?
No. Never. I’d never leave the kids.
How is this affecting home and work? And how does your partner see it?
We row every month. I hate how I am with the children. Then I feel guilty.
What have you been thinking is going on?
That I’m going mad. Or that I’m just a horrible person that week.
And what were you hoping for today?
For someone to take it seriously, and something that actually helps.

You’re not going mad and you’re not a horrible person. This looks like premenstrual dysphoric disorder, PMDD. It’s the severe form of premenstrual syndrome, where the brain is very sensitive to the normal hormone changes after ovulation. It’s recognised and it’s treatable.
To be sure, I’d like you to keep a daily symptom diary for two cycles. It shows the pattern clearly and checks it isn’t a low mood that’s there all month.
model.why: Prospective diary over two cycles (RCOG GTG 48)

model.text: Do I have to wait two months for help, though?
No. We can start treatment now and use the diary to see how well it works.
model.why: Responds to her need for action

model.text: There are two main medical options. One is an SSRI antidepressant, which is used for PMDD even when there’s no depression. You can take it every day, or only in the two weeks before your period. The other is a type of combined pill, often taken without breaks, to stop the hormone swings. Exercise and a talking therapy called CBT help too. What would suit you?
model.why: RCOG first-line options with shared decision

model.text: I’d rather not take hormones. The SSRI in the second half sounds good.

That’s a sensible choice. It’s commonly used for this, although it isn’t formally licensed for it. Some people feel a bit sick or more anxious in the first days. I’d like to speak to you again in a week to see how you are, given those darker thoughts.
Okay.
Let’s also make a plan for the bad days. What helps you get through them, and who could you tell if the thoughts got stronger?
My partner. I could tell him when it’s starting.

That’s a good plan. If those thoughts become stronger, or you feel you might act on them, contact us the same day, call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or 999 in an emergency. I’ll call you in a week, then see you after two cycles with the diary. Can you tell me the plan back?
Diary every day, tablets in the second half of my cycle, call in a week, and ring straight away if the thoughts get worse.

social.t: Monthly conflict affects her partner and children. With her consent, involving her partner helps both understanding and the safety plan.
Predictable monthly impairment may need workplace adjustments during the luteal phase.

legal.t: She describes snapping at her children, with guilt, not harm. This is a reason for support, not a safeguarding referral, unless there are concerns about the children’s safety; keep this under review.
SSRIs are unlicensed for premenstrual syndrome. Explain this and document the discussion (GMC prescribing guidance).

professional.t: Validation after dismissal is part of the treatment. Record the diagnosis clearly so she is not dismissed again.
Record her suicidal thoughts, the absence of plans or acts, protective factors and the safety plan, without a risk label (NICE NG225).

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies can provide CBT. PMDD charities offer information and peer support. Crisis lines and NHS 111 mental health option for bad days.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts with plans or intent
Symptoms persisting through the whole cycle (depression)
psychosocial: Guilt about how she is with her children
Feeling dismissed by a previous doctor
ice: Idea: going mad, or a horrible person that week
Concern: the depth of the lows; the effect on her family
Expectation: to be taken seriously and helped

playbook.diagnosis: “This looks like premenstrual dysphoric disorder, PMDD, the severe form of premenstrual syndrome. It’s real, recognised and treatable.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your hormone levels are normal, but your brain reacts strongly to the rise and fall after ovulation. That’s why you feel well after your period and unwell before the next one.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought you might be going mad. You’re not. This has a name and treatments that work.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the dismissal; address guilt; involve her partner in a safety plan with consent.
sharedPlan: Daily symptom diary for two cycles, for example DRSP (RCOG GTG 48)
SSRI in the luteal phase or continuously, unlicensed use, dose per BNF; or a new-generation combined pill if UKMEC allows
CBT and exercise; specialist referral if first- and second-line treatments fail
safetyNet: Stronger suicidal thoughts or any intent: same-day contact, NHS 111 mental health option, or 999
Review in 1 week after starting the SSRI (NICE NG222), then after two cycles with the diary
New agitation or mood elevation on the SSRI: seek review

pitfalls.intro: This station punishes the previous doctor’s mistake. The candidate must believe her, prove the pattern, find the suicidal thoughts behind “I frighten myself”, and offer real treatment.

items.why: Severe psychological symptoms with a symptom-free week and major impact fit PMDD.
She says she frightens herself; PMDD carries luteal-phase suicide risk.
items.fix: Ask directly and build a safety plan (NICE NG225).

items.why: RCOG GTG 48 recommends daily ratings over two cycles; recall is unreliable.
items.fix: Give a daily diary such as the DRSP.

items.fail: Missing a persistent mood disorder or bipolar disorder.
items.why: Depression with premenstrual worsening needs different treatment; SSRIs can trigger mania.
items.fix: Ask about the follicular week and elevated mood.

items.why: Options differ in hormones, contraception and timing.
items.fix: Lay out SSRI and combined pill options and let her choose.

items.why: She has suicidal thoughts and is starting an SSRI.
items.fix: Review within 1 week (NICE NG222) and give crisis routes.

timeMap.d: Let her finish. Acknowledge the previous dismissal.
Symptom-free week, luteal timing, physical symptoms, persistent or bipolar mood, suicidal thoughts and plans, impact on family and work.
“Going mad” and “a horrible person”. Name both.
PMDD by name; daily diary over two cycles; start treatment now.
SSRI or combined pill, CBT, exercise; safety plan; review in 1 week and after two cycles; crisis routes; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Repeats “it’s just PMS”; never asks about suicidal thoughts despite “I frighten myself”; offers evening primrose oil or nothing; no diary, no follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Recognises PMDD, asks about suicide, requests a symptom diary, offers an SSRI or combined pill and arranges review.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: tests for the symptom-free week and bipolar features; explores intent and protective factors calmly; explains PMDD in plain words; lets her choose between options, including luteal-phase SSRI dosing; builds a safety plan with her partner; arranges early review because of her thoughts; checks understanding with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Lots of women get moody before their period.”
avoid.instead: “What you describe is more than ordinary PMS. It’s a recognised condition called PMDD, and it’s treatable.”
avoid.why: She has been dismissed once already; minimising it damages trust and misses risk.

avoid.instead: “In those days, have you had thoughts of harming yourself, or that life isn’t worth living?”
avoid.why: A leading question invites a no; a direct open question is safer.

avoid.dont: “Come back when you’ve done two months of diary.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s start treatment now and use the diary to see how well it works.”
avoid.why: Her distress and risk justify starting treatment while the diary confirms the pattern.

Symptoms occur in the luteal phase, resolve by the end of menstruation, and are absent for at least a week in the follicular phase. PMDD is the severe, predominantly psychological form; the formal criteria are in DSM-5-TR [6] (international).

RCOG [1]: diagnose using prospective daily symptom ratings over two consecutive cycles, for example the Daily Record of Severity of Problems (DRSP). Retrospective recall is unreliable. A symptom-free week separates PMDD from depression or anxiety that worsens before periods.

Ask directly about suicidal thoughts and self-harm, especially in the luteal phase. NICE NG225 [2]: do not use risk tools or label risk as low, medium or high; agree a safety plan. Ask about bipolar symptoms before an SSRI.

RCOG [1] first-line options: exercise, CBT, vitamin B6, a new-generation combined oral contraceptive (drospirenone-containing pills usually more effective), taken cyclically or continuously, and low-dose SSRIs, given continuously or in the luteal phase only (days 15 to 28). SSRIs are unlicensed for PMS in the UK (dose per BNF [5]). Check UKMEC [4] before a combined pill: migraine with aura is UKMEC 4.
NICE NG222 [3]: review within 1 week of starting an antidepressant if at increased suicide risk. Withdraw gradually after continuous use; luteal-phase dosing avoids withdrawal effects.

RCOG [1]: second-line includes transdermal estradiol, off-label and usually with specialist advice (100 micrograms twice weekly is as effective as 200 micrograms) with cyclical progestogen or an LNG-IUS for endometrial protection. Specialist care for GnRH analogues (with add-back HRT if used beyond 6 months) and, rarely, surgery. Review after two to three cycles of each treatment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; acknowledged the previous dismissal.
Relationships, parenting, guilt and work explored.
Picked up “I’ve frightened myself with how low I get” and asked directly about suicidal thoughts.
Idea (going mad or a bad person), concern (the lows and the family), expectation (to be taken seriously and helped).
Prospective daily symptom diary over two cycles (RCOG GTG 48); no routine blood tests needed.
PMDD versus ordinary PMS, persistent depression or anxiety with premenstrual worsening, and bipolar disorder.
Suicidal thoughts, plans and self-harm explored; bipolar features screened before an SSRI.
Named PMDD as the severe form of premenstrual syndrome.
SSRI (luteal or continuous) or new-generation combined pill offered with CBT and exercise (RCOG GTG 48); her choice respected.
Guilt and impact on the family addressed; partner involved in the safety plan with her agreement.
Review in 1 week given suicidal thoughts (NICE NG222), then after two cycles; crisis routes given; teach-back.

social.t: Monthly conflict affects her partner and children. With her consent, involving her partner helps both understanding and the safety plan.
Predictable monthly impairment may need workplace adjustments during the luteal phase.

legal.t: She describes snapping at her children, with guilt, not harm. This is a reason for support, not a safeguarding referral, unless there are concerns about the children’s safety; keep this under review.
SSRIs are unlicensed for premenstrual syndrome. Explain this and document the discussion (GMC prescribing guidance).

professional.t: Validation after dismissal is part of the treatment. Record the diagnosis clearly so she is not dismissed again.
Record her suicidal thoughts, the absence of plans or acts, protective factors and the safety plan, without a risk label (NICE NG225).

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies can provide CBT. PMDD charities offer information and peer support. Crisis lines and NHS 111 mental health option for bad days.

Symptoms persisting through the whole cycle (depression)

Feeling dismissed by a previous doctor
ice: Idea: going mad, or a horrible person that week

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This looks like premenstrual dysphoric disorder, PMDD, the severe form of premenstrual syndrome. It’s real, recognised and treatable.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your hormone levels are normal, but your brain reacts strongly to the rise and fall after ovulation. That’s why you feel well after your period and unwell before the next one.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought you might be going mad. You’re not. This has a name and treatments that work.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the dismissal; address guilt; involve her partner in a safety plan with consent.
sharedPlan: Daily symptom diary for two cycles, for example DRSP (RCOG GTG 48)
SSRI in the luteal phase or continuously, unlicensed use, dose per BNF; or a new-generation combined pill if UKMEC allows
CBT and exercise; specialist referral if first- and second-line treatments fail
safetyNet: Stronger suicidal thoughts or any intent: same-day contact, NHS 111 mental health option, or 999
Review in 1 week after starting the SSRI (NICE NG222), then after two cycles with the diary
New agitation or mood elevation on the SSRI: seek review

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station punishes the previous doctor’s mistake. The candidate must believe her, prove the pattern, find the suicidal thoughts behind “I frighten myself”, and offer real treatment.

items.why: Severe psychological symptoms with a symptom-free week and major impact fit PMDD.
She says she frightens herself; PMDD carries luteal-phase suicide risk.
items.fix: Ask directly and build a safety plan (NICE NG225).

items.why: RCOG GTG 48 recommends daily ratings over two cycles; recall is unreliable.
items.fix: Give a daily diary such as the DRSP.

items.fail: Missing a persistent mood disorder or bipolar disorder.
items.why: Depression with premenstrual worsening needs different treatment; SSRIs can trigger mania.
items.fix: Ask about the follicular week and elevated mood.

items.why: Options differ in hormones, contraception and timing.
items.fix: Lay out SSRI and combined pill options and let her choose.

items.why: She has suicidal thoughts and is starting an SSRI.
items.fix: Review within 1 week (NICE NG222) and give crisis routes.
